newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sanyo Sec faces hard times if insurers reject plea.
newsitem.headline: Sanyo Sec faces hard times if insurers reject plea.

text.p: Second-tier Japanese brokerage Sanyo Securities Co Ltd may face tough times ahead if its request to delay repayment of its subordinated loans from life insurers is not accepted, industry sources said on Friday.

Unless the insurers accept the delay by the end of this month, Sanyo's capital adequacy ratio could fall below 120 percent, a level at which the Finance Ministry may order the brokerage to improve operations, the sources said.
Sanyo has a total of 20 billion yen in subordinated loans from nine life insurers which are due at the end of July 1998.
Subordinated loans cease to be regarded as part of an institution's capital once the remaining period to maturity falls below one year. At that point, the loans come to be treated as short-term debt.
On Friday, Yuzuru Fujita, president of Asahi Mutual Life Insurance Co, told reporters that the company has not yet decided about how to deal with the request from Sanyo.

"The current situation is different from the time when life insurers' assets rapidly increased. How to deal with subordinated loans must be judged by taking account of the risk stemming from such loans," he said.

Koichi Yoshida, president of Sumitomo Life Insurance Co, told the same conference: "We cannot accept the request unless Sanyo shows us a restructuring programme which clearly states how it plans to repay the subordinated loans."
Subordinated loans are repayable only after debts with higher claims have been honoured.
Despite their reluctance to agree to an extension of the subordinated loans, financial sources said the insurers would eventually accept the request.
"They will probably accept it," a financial source said. "If they don't, Sanyo's business may come under heavy pressure and it may end up failing to repay the subordinated loans."
Sanyo's financial woes stem from the bursting of the late 1980s economic bubble which left it burdened with bad assets at its financial and real estate affiliates.

In 1994 Sanyo worked out a nine-year restructuring programme to help bail out its non-bank affiliates including Sanyo Sogo Capital Co with the support of three major creditor banks and Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
The three banks were Nippon Credit Bank Ltd, Daiwa Bank Ltd and Bank of Tokyo, now Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd. In January 1995, nine life insurers also agreed to provide subordinated loans.
Sanyo had planned to help its affiliates write off their bad assets with profits from the brokerage.
But pressured by the protracted stock market slump, Sanyo has not recovered its profitability, posting parent net losses for a sixth consecutive year in 1996/97, ended March 31.
Sanyo has repeatedly said it expects the insurers to accept its request, and that it has no plans to change its restructuring programme.
